results.result: Six-month-old infants showed differential ERP responses to rare deviant stimuli (early, right-lateralized, 200-1000ms) and rare recombined stimuli (late, left-lateralized, 420-1000ms) compared to frequent standard stimuli, while adults only showed differential responses to rare deviant stimuli (180-1000ms) but not to rare recombined stimuli. This demonstrates that infants passively learned crossmodal conditional probabilities while adults did not under identical passive exposure conditions.
results.evaluation: The claims are supported by comprehensive ERP data from Experiment 1a (infants) and 1b (adults) with detailed statistical analyses (C71-C105). The experimental design appropriately controlled for stimulus element frequency by using recombined stimuli (C64, C144), allowing dissociation of element probability detection from conditional probability learning. Effect sizes (C110-C111) and power analyses (C108-C109, C112) support the conclusion that the null effect in adults was not due to insufficient power. The topographic and temporal patterns are clearly documented in Figures 1-2.

results.result: Adults showed differential ERP responses to rare recombined stimuli versus frequent standard stimuli only when crossmodal combinations were task-relevant (Experiment 2b) but not when they were task-irrelevant (Experiment 2a), despite showing sensitivity to rare deviant stimuli in both conditions. This demonstrates that adult learning of crossmodal statistics depends on task relevance.
results.evaluation: The claims are well-supported by ERP data from Experiments 2a and 2b with appropriate experimental manipulation of task relevance. Behavioral data (C115-C123) confirms participants attended to stimuli in both experiments. The critical comparison shows adults can learn crossmodal statistics when motivated by task demands (C133-C134), replicating the null finding from Experiment 1b with improved design (C113). This provides converging evidence for the developmental difference in learning mechanisms.

results.result: The study demonstrates heightened sensitivity for crossmodal statistics in six-month-old infants compared to adults, indicating a developmental change in learning mode from passive implicit learning in infancy to task-dependent learning in adulthood. Infants learned arbitrary crossmodal associations earlier than previously reported (six months vs. twelve months).
results.evaluation: This overarching conclusion is well-supported by the convergent evidence from all four experiments (C2-C5, C135-C136). The claims appropriately synthesize the experimental findings and extend previous research (C140-C142, C150-C152). The conclusion is strengthened by appropriate controls for stimulus frequency (C144), dissociation of different learning processes (C145-C149), and replication across multiple experiments with different designs (C113-C114). The inference of developmental change in learning mechanisms is justified by the systematic pattern of results.

results.result: The experimental design successfully dissociated processing of element probabilities (frequent vs. rare deviant stimuli) from processing of conditional probabilities of crossmodal combinations (frequent standard vs. rare recombined stimuli). All groups showed sensitivity to rare deviant stimuli with early ERP effects consistent with mismatch negativity, while only infants showed later effects for rare recombined stimuli.
results.evaluation: The experimental design logic is sound (C64, C144, C194-C195) and the dissociation is empirically demonstrated (C192-C193, C196). The interpretation of early deviant effects as reflecting unisensory memory traces (C197-C200) is reasonable and supported by citations to MMN literature. This methodological contribution allows clear interpretation of the developmental differences observed. The claims appropriately distinguish what the design can and cannot test (C199, C204).

results.result: The study tested the hypothesis that six-month-old infants can learn arbitrary auditory-visual associations and show higher sensitivity to crossmodal statistics compared to adults during passive exposure, predicting ERP differences for rare deviant stimuli in both groups but ERP differences for rare recombined stimuli only in infants.
results.evaluation: The hypotheses were clearly stated a priori (C62-C63, C65-C66) and were supported by the experimental results. The predictions were appropriately grounded in prior literature (C65 cites relevant MMN studies). The hypothesis about developmental differences was novel and the experimental design was appropriate to test it. The results confirmed both predictions, demonstrating good experimental planning and execution.

results.result: The null effect for rare recombined stimuli in adults (Experiment 1b) was not due to insufficient signal-to-noise ratio or statistical power, as evidenced by detection of smaller effects (rare deviant stimuli) and replication of the null effect in Experiment 2a with improved signal-to-noise.
results.evaluation: The authors appropriately addressed a potential alternative explanation (C154) and provided multiple lines of evidence against it (C155, C112). The effect size comparisons (C110-C111) and replication in Experiment 2a with better signal-to-noise strengthen this conclusion. This demonstrates careful consideration of methodological limitations and appropriate follow-up experiments.

results.result: The left-lateralized ERP effect for rare recombined stimuli in infants may reflect recruitment of neural circuits involved in language-related statistical learning (conditional probability detection), while the right-lateralized effect for rare deviant stimuli in passive conditions may reflect reflexive attention orienting that is suppressed during active task engagement.
results.evaluation: These interpretations are speculative (C203, C207-C208, C212) though grounded in relevant literature (C205-C206, C209, C213). The lateralization patterns are empirically observed (C68-C70, C210-C211) but the functional interpretations go beyond what the data directly demonstrate. The claims appropriately acknowledge the speculative nature and cite supporting literature, but additional experiments would be needed to test these specific mechanistic hypotheses. The surprise expressed about lateralization in infants (C203) suggests this was not fully anticipated.

results.result: The developmental change in crossmodal learning may reflect a transition from extensive initial crossmodal connectivity that allows passive learning during sensitive periods to more selective, task-dependent plasticity in adulthood mediated by elaborated feedback connections and higher-order neural systems, consistent with findings from animal models of developmental plasticity.
results.evaluation: This is a speculative mechanistic framework (C180-C185, C190-C191) that integrates the present findings with animal literature (C174, C186-C188) and theoretical models (C175-C176, C182-C183). While the speculation is well-grounded in cited literature and consistent with the present results (C189), it goes well beyond what the ERP data can directly demonstrate. The claims appropriately acknowledge the speculative nature and cite relevant supporting work, but the proposed neural mechanisms would require additional neuroimaging or neurophysiological studies to test directly. This represents reasonable theoretical integration rather than empirically demonstrated results.

results.result: The finding of enhanced implicit learning in infants compared to adults is consistent with some prior studies showing superior statistical learning in children, though other studies have found the opposite pattern. These different outcomes may relate to task complexity, working memory demands, and the distinction between simple conditional probabilities versus higher-order statistical patterns.
results.evaluation: The authors appropriately contextualize their findings within mixed prior literature (C157-C164) and offer reasonable explanations for discrepant findings (C165-C169). The speculation about declining sensitivity to simple conditional probabilities (C171-C172) is grounded in cited work (C170). This represents good scholarly practice in acknowledging complexity in the literature and proposing testable explanations for inconsistencies. However, the explanations remain speculative (C165, C168) and would benefit from direct empirical testing.

results.result: ERP effects in adults showed different polarity and shorter latency compared to infants, which is consistent with known developmental differences in brain maturation (incomplete myelination) and commonly reported polarity differences between infant and adult ERPs.
results.evaluation: The empirical observation of polarity and latency differences is clearly documented (C215). The interpretation is appropriately grounded in established developmental neuroscience knowledge (C217) and cited literature (C218). The authors appropriately acknowledge these differences and explain their approach to linking effects across age groups (C216). This demonstrates appropriate handling of a common challenge in developmental ERP research.

results.result: The study included appropriate sample sizes with 29 six-month-old infants (Experiment 1a), 23 adults (Experiment 1b), and 12 adults (Experiments 2a/2b) after exclusions for artifacts or poor task performance. The ~50% exclusion rate in infants is typical for infant ERP research. Ethical approval was obtained.
results.evaluation: The participant information is clearly documented (C224-C226, C230-C235) with appropriate inclusion criteria (C225) and justified exclusions (C226-C227, C231, C234). The sample sizes are reasonable for ERP studies, particularly given the clear effects observed. The high infant exclusion rate is appropriately contextualized as typical (C227). Ethical procedures are documented (C228-C229). However, the relatively small sample in Experiment 2 (n=12) is a limitation, though the clear effects suggest adequate power for the main comparisons.
